title: Pity is not compassion
hookLine: compassion's near enemy is pity or sorrow; its far enemy is cruelty (Visuddhimagga 9)
tomorrow: Compassion for the one who harms

cards: Have you ever been on the receiving end of the head tilt? You share something hard, and the other person tilts their head, lowers their voice, and says, oh, you poor thing. They mean well.

But the one on the receiving end can feel smaller: they came as an equal and somehow left as a charity case. Compare the friend who just sits down next to you and says, that's awful, I'm here. Both are responses to pain.
Only one of them feels like company.

teach.b: Like every room, compassion has two enemies. The Visuddhimagga names the far enemy first: cruelty, the wish to hurt, the plain opposite of the trembling heart. That one's easy to spot.
The near enemy is trickier. The manual's word for it is grief, a sorrow tied to one's own worldly life, domanassa. It's near because both compassion and grief see someone's misfortune.
But grief turns the pain toward yourself: how awful, how sad this makes me. Compassion keeps its eyes on the other person, and on what would help.
So the manual says compassion succeeds when it makes cruelty fade, and fails when it just produces sorrow. Some modern teachers add a close cousin: pity.

teach.h: PITY LOOKS DOWN FROM A SAFE HEIGHT.
teach.b: Pity also sees misfortune, but it looks down from a safe height. It says, I'm glad that's not me. It keeps a little distance, a little ranking, between the one who suffers and the one who feels sorry.
Compassion closes that distance. It knows the same things can happen to anyone: sickness, loss, old age, death. Remember the sick monk.
The Buddha didn't stand in the doorway looking sad.
He had water fetched, and with Ananda washed the man with his own hands and lifted him onto a bed.
Beside him, not above. There's a simple test. After you meet someone's pain, do you feel smaller and more burdened, or more connected and more ready to help?
The first is sorrow. The second is the room called karuna.

how: Meditation teachers use the Visuddhimagga's near and far enemies to help students tell compassion from sorrow and pity; some Buddhist chaplains and caregivers describe their work as being present beside someone rather than rescuing from above.

o: sorrow that turns another's pain toward yourself
anger at the people who caused someone's pain
a calm acceptance that suffering is part of life

games.q: match each piece of compassion's map.
p: looks down from a safe height

s: the manual names cruelty as compassion's far enemy
it's the plain opposite of the trembling heart.
feeling very sad about someone's pain is always compassion
the manual says compassion fails when it only produces sorrow.
the manual's own word for the near enemy is pity
its word is grief, domanassa; some modern teachers add pity as a close cousin.

games.q: a friend tells you they've lost their job. which response is compassion, by the manual's map?
o: 'oh, you poor thing. glad it wasn't me.'
'that's awful. I'm here. what would help?'
games.why: pity looks down; grief turns the pain toward yourself; compassion stays beside the other person and looks for what would help.

practice: Bring back the person you thought of yesterday, and notice where you stand in the picture: looking down at them, a little sorry and a little relieved, or sinking into your own sadness?
Gently change the picture: sit down beside them, shoulder to shoulder, on the same ground. From there, offer the wish: may you be free from this pain.

wordCard.voice: Domanassa. Grief, a sorrow tied to our own worldly life: compassion's near enemy, sorrow that turns inward, and pity that looks down; compassion sits beside.

orig.note: Pali domanassa: grief, sorrow; the Visuddhimagga's near enemy of compassion.

carryVoice: Your line: beside, not above. Same ground, same kind of life, shoulder to shoulder. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga IX (karuna: near enemy, far enemy, success and failure)
